Trauma-Sensitive / Restorative Yoga

Whether yoga settles you or makes things worse can depend a lot on what kind of yoga you are doing. Keep in mind that power yoga, hot yoga, and so forth are not what I mean here; I mean trauma-sensitive yoga, restorative yoga, gentle somatic yoga, or sometimes very gentle yin. If a teacher tells you to open your hips and release your trauma, that does not necessarily mean the class is trauma-informed. Sometimes the slowest, easiest-to-leave version is the useful one.

With yin I would use props and keep the holds short. One obvious question is whether you still have choices while you are in the pose. Can you keep your eyes open, come out whenever you want, and say that a sensation is useful, neutral, or too much? Can the posture have more than one correct version, depending on your body?

I would avoid intense stretching, forced breathwork or breath retention, aggressive hip openers, long passive holds that you have to endure, and hands-on adjustments without clear consent. Pushing through is not the point of this kind of yoga. You have to retain the choice while you are actually doing it.

EMDR

Whether EMDR is the right place to start can depend a lot on whether you can point to the memory. Keep in mind that an accident, an assault memory, military trauma, one distinct flashback, or a specific network of triggers all give you a fairly clear target. If somebody is stable and has one clear event, that does not necessarily mean they need months of body work first. Sometimes EMDR is the obvious early choice.

Brainspotting is easier to feel your way into when you do not know exactly what you are looking for; with EMDR, the target and recall procedure are clearer. I become more cautious when the trauma is diffuse or developmental, mostly bodily or pre-verbal, relational, or the person's nervous system is still unstable. In those cases I would want at least some access to a Nurturer and Protector before opening very charged material, and Brainspotting may fit earlier.

Sky Hypnosis and Vagal Blitz

Whether Sky Hypnosis or Vagal Blitz is useful can depend a lot on how well you can stay present and come back afterward. Keep in mind that these are deliberately intense state-shifters, not ordinary regulation practices, and they are not prerequisites for healing. If somebody is stable they may still find one useful before doing the therapies above. Sometimes the unusual practice really is the thing that helps, but I still need to be able to stop voluntarily.

Sky Hypnosis can make you lightheaded. Vagal Blitz has to be done lying down and has cardiovascular and mental-health cautions. I would read the complete guide, begin with the least intense version that gives a useful shift, and stop if balance, orientation, or recovery becomes unreliable. Fainting and loss of consciousness are not the goal.

One obvious question is what happens later. When I remember the event, am I actually less restimulated, and am I any better at pain, boundaries, conflict, and ordinary life? A huge release, bliss, or an altered state does not answer that. If I am mainly using the practice to avoid grief, conflict, practical problems, or deeper relational healing, the extraordinary state is not doing what I needed it to do.
